EUropean Consensus on the Resolution Of SympToms After Oesophago-gastric Resection (EUROSTAR)
  • Source: Gut 2026;0:1–15. doi:10.1136/gutjnl-2025-337109
  • Topic: Postoperative symptom management after upper gastrointestinal cancer surgery
  • Author(s): Barman S, Chevallay M, Gisbertz SS, et al. (EUROSTAR Study Faculty Members)
Overview of Symptoms After UGI Cancer Surgery
  • Symptoms are common and significantly affect quality of life
  • Treatment often includes chemo(radio)therapy + surgery → irreversible changes to GI tract anatomy/physiology
  • Symptoms are often multiple and under-appreciated
  • Routine postoperative symptom monitoring is not standard of care in most centres
  • Patients may feel unsupported dealing with these consequences
Symptom Burden Statistics
  • Patients typically have 10–13 symptoms after UGI cancer surgery
  • Symptoms can migrate over time from upper GI (early) to lower GI (late)
  • Beyond 1 year post-surgery, high symptom burden persists
  • Symptoms cluster and adversely affect quality of life
Service Provision & Follow-Up Recommendations
Core Principles
  • Systematic approach to assessment, investigation, and management --> faster symptom resolution → improved quality of life
  • Given significant symptom overlap between conditions, testing is recommended prior to treatment
  • Empirical treatment may be considered for certain conditions --> response to treatment must be documented
  • Changes to GI tract from surgery, oncological treatments (chemo/radiotherapy/immunotherapy), medications, and pre-existing conditions --> all contribute to symptoms
Follow-Up Model
  • Optimal follow-up model is unknown
  • May combine routine face-to-face, remote/virtual, and 'as required' (patient/questionnaire initiated) contacts
  • Follow-up should be individualized after surgery and may need to be long-term in some patients
Multidisciplinary Team (MDT)
  • Timely availability of MDT expertise is beneficial
  • Includes: upper GI surgery, gastroenterology, oncology (medical and clinical/radiation), nursing, dietetics, psychology, allied health professionals
  • Access to MDT meeting for complex cases is recommended
  • Access to key investigations at point of care is desirable
Clinical Assessment
  • Full history including dietary history --> recommended
  • Pattern and timing of symptoms must be documented
  • Consider underlying pre-existing conditions
Nutritional Management
  • Nutritional issues are common --> specialist dietitian input during follow-up is recommended
  • Weight loss and micronutrient deficiency are common
  • Monitoring for micronutrient requirements --> mitigate risk of deficiencies
Specific Supplementation Recommendations
  • Complete multivitamin/mineral supplement (containing iron, selenium, zinc, copper) --> recommended for all post-oesophagectomy/gastrectomy patients
  • Combined calcium and vitamin D supplement --> should be considered (weak recommendation)
  • Long-term vitamin B12 supplementation (parenteral) --> recommended for all post-total gastrectomy patients
  • Vitamin B12 monitoring and supplementation --> appropriate after subtotal gastrectomy or oesophagectomy
Symptom Monitoring Tools
  • Symptom questionnaires (patient-reported outcome measures) --> recommended to document symptom burden and trajectory
  • Contemporaneous recording of symptomatic response to treatment --> provides efficacy information and likelihood of diagnosis being correct
Diagnostic Criteria & Investigation Pathways
General Principles
  • Symptoms are a prerequisite for investigation and intervention
  • Conditions can be asymptomatic or subclinical (absence of symptoms does not preclude underlying condition)
  • Validated, objective symptom questionnaires + tailored patient history --> recommended
  • Testing generally considered preferable for definitive diagnosis
  • Many conditions often treated empirically
  • Prospective symptom response to treatment --> good indicator of correct diagnosis in clinical practice or outcome measure in trials
Acid Reflux (GORD)
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Typical symptoms: retrosternal chest pain/burning, reflux/heartburn, regurgitation, acid in mouth, gravity-dependent reflux/regurgitation
  • Atypical symptoms: cough, hoarse voice

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND either:

  • Conclusive evidence of GORD at endoscopy (Los Angeles classification grade A–D)
  • OR pathological oesophageal acid exposure on pH monitoring (acid exposure time >6%)

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to adequate acid suppression therapy

First-Line Investigation
  • Upper GI endoscopy/OGD (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Treatment Ladder
  • First-line: Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Second-line: H2 receptor antagonist (e.g., famotidine) (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Adjunct: Alginates (e.g., Gaviscon Advanced) --> evidence-based adjunct to acid suppressing medication
Non-Acid (Bile) Reflux
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Retrosternal chest pain/burning, reflux/heartburn, regurgitation, burning in mouth, cough, nocturnal/postural symptoms
  • Bitter taste of bile in mouth --> highly suggestive

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND evidence of inflammation and bile in oesophagus or stomach at endoscopy

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

First-Line Investigation
  • Upper GI endoscopy/OGD (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Second-Line Investigation
  • Oesophageal impedance monitoring (very low evidence, weak recommendation)
Treatment Ladder
  • First-line: Sucralfate suspension (6-week trial sufficient to assess benefit) (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Second-line (weak support): Alginates, prokinetic agents, ursodeoxycholic acid, topical anaesthetic agents (e.g., oxetacaine/mucaine)
Anastomotic Stricture
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Dysphagia (score ≥2), odynophagia, regurgitation, nausea/vomiting, early satiety (especially gastrectomy), reduced dietary intake, weight loss, chest pain

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND either:

  • Anastomotic stricture on OGD: severe = inability to pass 8–10 mm diagnostic gastroscope; moderate = clear narrowing but able to pass standard scope
  • OR anastomotic stricture on contrast study: severe = hold-up/proximal dilation ≤10 mm; moderate = >10 mm

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

First-Line Investigation
  • Upper GI endoscopy/OGD (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Second-Line Investigation
  • Liquid barium/water-soluble contrast study (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Treatment Ladder
  • First-line: Balloon (or bougie) dilatation (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Second-line: Dilatation with steroid injection OR endoscopic stricturoplasty (needle-knife incision) (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
Delayed Gastric Emptying (DGE)
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, early satiety, regurgitation, reduced dietary intake, weight loss, heartburn, acid/bile in mouth, abdominal/chest pain, belching

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND either:

  • Significant food/liquid residue in stomach on OGD despite fasting
  • OR delayed passage of contrast on timed barium/water-soluble swallow and meal (determined by expert GI radiologist)
  • OR delayed emptying on gastric emptying study (determined by expert radiologist/physiologist)

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

Note: Normal range values need to be established in UGI cancer surgery patients

First-Line Investigations
  • Upper GI endoscopy/OGD (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Timed liquid barium/water-soluble contrast study (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Second-Line Investigation
  • Gastric emptying study (very low evidence, weak recommendation)
Treatment Ladder
First-Line Treatments
  • Endoscopic pyloric dilatation (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Short-term/intermittent use of prokinetic drugs (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Prokinetic Drug Options
Drug Dose Duration Cautions
Metoclopramide 10 mg TDS before meals 3 months Risk of tardive dyskinesia >3 months
Erythromycin (syrup) 250–500 mg TDS before meals 6 weeks Tachyphylaxis after 6 weeks; electrolyte disturbances
Domperidone 10 mg TDS orally 1 week ↑ risk of ventricular arrhythmia; cardiac side effects
Aprepitant 125 mg once daily 4 weeks No cautions; safe long-term
Prucalopride 2 mg once daily Long-term if required Cautions if cardiac arrhythmias/ischaemic heart disease
Paroxetine 20 mg once daily 6 months initially Can ↑ bleeding risk
Second-Line Treatments
  • Surgical pyloroplasty (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Botulinum toxin type A injection of pylorus (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Pneumatic dilatation (e.g., larger balloon up to 30 mm) (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
Third-Line Treatment
  • Gastric per oral endoscopic myotomy (GPOEM) within research setting (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Dumping Syndrome
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Postprandial abdominal pain, bloating, borborygmi, nausea, diarrhoea, flushing, palpitations, perspiration, tachycardia, hypotension, fatigue, desire to lie down, syncope

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND if oral glucose tolerance test performed:

  • Early dumping: rise in haematocrit >3% OR rise in heart rate >10 bpm at 30 min
  • Late dumping: hypoglycaemia (<3.3 mmol/L) at 60–180 min after ingestion

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

First-Line Investigation
  • Food and symptom diary, thorough dietary history (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
Second-Line Investigation
  • Modified oral glucose tolerance test (75 g glucose in water after overnight fast with blood glucose, haematocrit, pulse, BP before and at 30 min intervals up to 3 hours) (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
Third-Line Investigation
  • Continuous glucose monitoring (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Treatment Ladder
  • First-line: Dietary advice by specialist dietitian (reduced meal size, food/fluid separation, high fibre/high protein diet) (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Second-line: Octreotide for early dumping (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Third-line: Acarbose for late dumping (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Bile Acid Diarrhoea (BAD)
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Diarrhoea, bloating, abdominal pain/cramps, flatulence, incontinence, faecal urgency, nocturnal diarrhoea, borborygmi, frequency of defecation, fatigue, weight loss

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND positive 75-selenium homocholic acid taurine (SeHCAT) scan:

  • Borderline: 15–20% residual bile acid
  • Mild: 10–15%
  • Moderate: 5–10%
  • Severe: <5%

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

First-Line Investigation
  • SeHCAT scan (high evidence, strong recommendation)

Note: 7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (7C4) is being investigated as screening tool but not yet established in surgical patients

Treatment Ladder
  • First-line: Bile acid sequestrants (e.g., colesevelam, colestyramine, colestipol) + reduced fat intake (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Second-line: Antidiarrhoeal agents (e.g., loperamide) (moderate evidence, weak recommendation)
Carbohydrate Malabsorption
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, flatulence, brain fog, frequency of defecation

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND (having excluded SIBO):

  • Positive breath test: rise in hydrogen ≥20 ppm from baseline during fructose/lactose breath testing

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

First-Line Investigation Options
  • Empirical 14-day trial of specific carbohydrate exclusion (e.g., lactose-free diet) as diagnostic manoeuvre (low evidence, weak recommendation)
  • OR fructose/lactose breath test (low evidence, weak recommendation)
First-Line Treatment
  • Dietary exclusion of carbohydrates under specialist dietitian supervision (moderate evidence, strong recommendation)
Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhoea, constipation, reduced dietary intake, weight loss, flatulence, steatorrhoea, borborygmi, faecal urgency, nausea, vomiting, early satiety, dyspepsia, heartburn, belching, brain fog, fatigue, headache, muscle aches

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND either:

  • Positive breath test: rise ≥20 ppm from baseline in hydrogen in 90 min OR ≥10 ppm for methane
  • OR excessive bacteria (>10³ CFU/mL from small bowel aspirate)
  • OR growth of colonic/atypical bacteria on small bowel aspirate

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to antibiotics

First-Line Investigation
  • Breath test (recommended) (moderate evidence, weak recommendation)
Alternative Investigation
  • Small bowel (duodenal/jejunal) aspirate with cultures (low evidence, weak recommendation)
Breath Test Substrate Considerations
Substrate Characteristics
Lactulose Non-absorbable --> liable to false positives due to colonic fermentation in fast transit
Glucose Rapidly absorbed in proximal small bowel --> risks false negatives in distal SIBO/IMO
Treatment Ladder
First-Line Management
  • Antibiotics (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Second-Line Management
  • Alternative antibiotics (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Third-Line Management
  • Probiotics, prokinetics, FODMAP diet, correct reversible causes (very low evidence, weak recommendation)
Antibiotic Options for SIBO
Antimicrobial Indication Target Duration
Rifaximin First-line for SIBO, especially hydrogen-dominant cases Primarily gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria 7–14 days
Co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin/norfloxacin Resistant cases where rifaximin ineffective; mixed infections (gram+, gram−, anaerobes) Various 7–14 days
Neomycin + rifaximin Methane-dominant SIBO/IMO --> combination more effective than single agent Gram-negative (especially methanogens) and some gram-positive 7–14 days
Vancomycin Methane-dominant cases Gram-negative and methanogens 7–14 days
Metronidazole Resistant cases or complicated SIBO Anaerobes 7–14 days

Note: Oral iron supplementation can fuel methanogens and dysbiotic bacteria --> exacerbate symptoms

Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency (EPI)
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Suggestive symptoms: Weight loss, steatorrhoea, urgency, bloating, foul-smelling stool/flatus, abdominal pain, diarrhoea

Diagnosis requires:

1. Suggestive symptoms

2. AND low faecal elastase (<200 μg/g of faeces)

3. AND/OR symptomatic response to treatment

Note: Low faecal elastase does not always correlate with proven fat malabsorption; functional insufficiency can occur --> diagnosis may still be considered with typical symptoms alone or indeterminate levels (200–500 μg/g)

First-Line Investigation
  • Faecal elastase level (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Assessment After Diagnosis
  • Comprehensive nutritional assessment including fat-soluble vitamin status (A, D, E, K)
First-Line Treatment
  • Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (e.g., Creon, Nutrizym, Pancrease, Pancrex) + dietary advice (high evidence, strong recommendation)

Response assessment: 4 weeks appropriate period if adequate compliance, patient education, and dosage

Recurrent Cancer
Diagnostic Criteria
  • Endoscopic, histopathological, or radiological evidence of recurrent disease
Concerning Symptoms (Deviation from Postoperative Baseline)
  • Luminal symptoms: Dysphagia, anorexia, regurgitation, vomiting
  • Non-luminal symptoms: Weight loss (>10%), abdominal/chest pain, lethargy/fatigue, progressive hoarse voice, jaundice, malaise
First-Line Investigation
  • Luminal symptoms: Upper GI endoscopy/OGD + CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis (high evidence, strong recommendation)
  • Non-luminal symptoms: CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis (high evidence, strong recommendation)
Management
  • Discussion and agreement at local MDT meeting (strong recommendation)
Research Priorities Identified
Symptom Assessment & Monitoring

1. What is the symptom burden in this patient group?

2. Can PROMs prospectively document symptom burden?

Nutrition & Micronutrients

3. Role of routine vs targeted micronutrient supplementation (including bone health)

4. Optimal frequency of vitamin B12 injections

5. Efficacy of oral vitamin B12 administration after UGI surgery

Reflux Management

6. Optimal treatment for bile reflux

Stricture Treatment

7. Comparison of dilatation vs dilatation + steroid injection vs needle-knife stricturoplasty for anastomotic stricture

Gastric Emptying

8. Normal range values for contrast studies or gastric emptying studies specifically after UGI surgery

9. Comparison of dilatation vs dilatation + Botox vs surgical pyloroplasty vs GPOEM for delayed gastric conduit emptying

Bile Acid Diarrhoea

10. Role of bile acid sequestrants and optimal choice (especially for borderline SeHCAT results)

11. Role and efficacy of low-fat diet for BAD

SIBO & Carbohydrate Malabsorption

12. Normal range values for breath testing specifically after oesophagogastric cancer surgery and optimal substrate

13. Sensitivity and role of small bowel aspirates in diagnosing SIBO

14. Role of probiotics, prokinetics, and dietary manipulation (e.g., low FODMAP diet) for SIBO

Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency

15. Role of PERT in patients with borderline/negative faecal elastase (200–500 μg/g or >500 μg/g)

16. Role of empirical PERT treatment for steatorrhoea presumed to be EPI

17. Duration of trial period and when to stop if no clinical response (4 weeks)

Cancer Surveillance

18. Symptom-driven vs routine/intensive surveillance for recurrence
